description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
B.1.1 About 2/3 of the participants had successfully finished the training at the deadline. However, training material and exercises etc. are still available on the FutureWater Moodle School platform for the other participants, but also for the new to be hired staff. All the participants indicated that the Moodle platform was very useful and that most of them were working on the exercises at a moment that suited them best. Participants also indicated that they would try to finish the training after the deadline. It was also indicated that new staff will be asked to work on the exercises and training material that we have developed and made available on our Moodle platform. It is therefore expected that most of the current participants, but also new staff will finish the training in the coming year.
B.1.4. From all 12 participants that followed the training, 2 were women and 10 were man. From the participants that finished the training at the deadline, also 2 were women and 6 were man. This indicates that gender unfortunately was not too balanced, but the women that did participate were very active and did not hesitate to ask questions and speak up.
B.1.8 We've shared the survey results under B.1.8 but generally speaking, all participants indicated that they learned something new. Sometimes it was completely new, sometimes it was something that a few participants already were familiar with. The new skills that were obtained by the participants can really help them in understanding and quantifying climate smart irrigation strategies in Iraq in more detail.
B.O.1. The number of organizations strengthened in this training is firstly the university of Basra, since their staff were the ones that participated in the training. However, also staff from other universities joined the training (Anbar, Mosul, Salahaddin) so the knowledge and skills acquired are spread over multiple knowledge institutions. FutureWater and Wageningen University were also strengthened by this group training, because we had to adapt to the COVID-19 situation and had to provide an online training course instead of on-site. This challenged us as well and we had to adapt and learn along the way of the training.
Revision note: Because of Covid-19 we had no choice other than provide an online training, but as stated previously in this case the remote format was not a good match with the more advanced topics offered, as this training was envisioned as a follow-up (deepening) to a larger TMT+ project (OKP-IRA-104278). In hindsight this may have been not the best setup to go for

comment.narrative:
11-10-2022: Basra university is a public institute, and we received some very positive feedback on the training. The participants indicated that they've learned a lot from the training. We can also say that we at FutureWater (private) and Wageningen University (public) learned a lot from the training too, since we were dealing with a completely new situation (COVID 19) and had to adapt our training material & methods to be effective for an e-learning environment
Revision note: We may have misinterpreted this question and thought it would only apply to the organizations involved in providing the training. The affiliations of the participants were from the following universities: Salahaddin, Mosul, Kufa, Basrah and Anbar. So in that respect we may have reached a total of 6 public organizations (including WUR) and 1 private (FutureWater). One participant from the Ministry of Agriculture (Office of Agricultural Extension and Training) participated partly in the training (not completed) so we fell short in the goal of strengthening 2 government agencies.

title.narrative: B.I.1. Number of scholarship holders / TMT participants that have successfully completed course/training (male / female / minorities)

comment.narrative:
11-10-2022: We set out to have at least 20 (10 F /10 M) participants to successfully complete the training, but we have been unable to fully accomplish this. Primarily we have been unable to attract enough female participants to the training. We were able to sign up a fair number of people (33 total, 14F) but this didn't translate unfortunately in full attendance and passing of the course.
Revision note: That we were unsuccessful in accomplishing our goal of training at least 20 people was in our opinion due to various reasons. Looking back into our Moodle system, we can see that at least 23 people have activated and accessed the course. Of those 23 people 17 have actually attended 1 or more training session, but in the end only 12 completed the training. We think it was a combination of both the online setup of the training and the relatively difficulty of the topics that we lost people along the way. Some concepts or modules would definitely have benefited from an in-person setup, but that was not possible due to Covid and travel restrictions., Also internet issues were raised by some people. We tried to keep engaging people to keep attendance high, but also that was difficult to accomplish. People joined from their homes and were quite easily distracted we found
